In [[vector calculus]], a '''complex lamellar vector field''' is a [[vector field]] which is orthogonal to a family of surfaces. In the broader context of [[differential geometry]], complex lamellar vector fields are more often called '''hypersurface-orthogonal vector fields.''' They can be characterized in a number of different ways, many of which involve the [[curl (mathematics)|curl]]. A '''lamellar vector field''' is a special case given by vector fields with zero curl.

The adjective "lamellar" derives from the noun "lamella", which means a thin layer. The ''lamellae'' to which "lamellar vector field" refers are the surfaces of constant potential, or in the complex case, the surfaces orthogonal to the vector field.{{sfnm|1a1=Panton|1y=2013|1p=434}}

==Complex lamellar vector fields==
In [[vector calculus]], a '''complex lamellar vector field''' is a [[vector field]] in three dimensions which is [[orthogonality|orthogonal]] to its own [[curl (mathematics)|curl]].{{sfnm|1a1=Aris|1y=1962|1p=64|2a1=Panton|2y=2013|2loc=Section 17.4}} That is,

:<math>\mathbf{F}\cdot (\nabla\times \mathbf{F}) = 0.</math>

The term '''lamellar vector field''' is sometimes used as a synonym for the special case of an [[irrotational vector field]], meaning that{{sfnm|1a1=Aris|1y=1962|1p=64}}
:<math>\nabla\times\mathbf{F}=\mathbf{0}.</math>

Complex lamellar vector fields are precisely those that are normal to a family of surfaces. An irrotational vector field is locally the [[gradient]] of a function, and is therefore orthogonal to the family of [[level surface]]s (the [[equipotential surface]]s).{{sfnm|1a1=Aris|1y=1962|1p=66}} Any vector field can be decomposed as the sum of an irrotational vector field and a complex lamellar field.{{sfnm|1a1=Aris|1y=1962|1p=72|2a1=Panton|2y=2013|2loc=Section 17.4}}

==Hypersurface-orthogonal vector fields==
In greater generality, a vector field {{math|'''F'''}} on a [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold]] is said to be '''hypersurface-orthogonal''' if through an arbitrary point there is a [[embedded submanifold|smoothly embedded hypersurface]] which, at all of its points, is orthogonal to the vector field. By the [[Frobenius theorem (differential topology)|Frobenius theorem]] this is equivalent to requiring that the [[Lie bracket of vector fields|Lie bracket]] of any smooth vector fields orthogonal to {{math|'''F'''}} is still orthogonal to {{math|'''F'''}}.{{sfnm|1a1=O'Neill|1y=1983|1loc=Proposition 12.30}}

The condition of hypersurface-orthogonality can be rephrased in terms of the [[differential form|differential 1-form]] {{math|&omega;}} which is dual to {{math|'''F'''}}. The previously given Lie bracket condition can be reworked to require that the [[exterior derivative]] {{math|d&omega;}}, when evaluated on any two tangent vectors which are orthogonal to {{math|'''F'''}}, is zero.{{sfnm|1a1=O'Neill|1y=1983|1loc=Proposition 12.30}} This may also be phrased as the requirement that there is a smooth 1-form whose [[wedge product]] with {{math|&omega;}} equals {{math|d&omega;}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Lee|1y=2013|1loc=Lemma 19.6}}

Alternatively, this may be written as the condition that the [[differential form|differential 3-form]] {{math|&omega; ∧ d&omega;}} is zero. This can also be phrased, in terms of the [[Levi-Civita connection]] defined by the metric, as requiring that the totally anti-symmetric part of the 3-tensor field {{math|&omega;<sub>''i''</sub>∇<sub>''j'' </sub>&omega;<sub>''k''</sub>}} is zero.{{sfnm|1a1=Wald|1y=1984|1loc=Appendix B.3}} Using a different formulation of the Frobenius theorem, it is also equivalent to require that {{math|&omega;}} is locally expressible as {{math|&lambda; d''u''}} for some functions {{math|&lambda;}} and {{mvar|u}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Flanders|1y=1989|1pp=96–97|2a1=Stephani|2a2=Kramer|2a3=MacCallum|2a4=Hoenselaers|2y=2003|2p=68}}

In the special case of vector fields on [[Euclidean space|three-dimensional Euclidean space]], the hypersurface-orthogonal condition is equivalent to the complex lamellar condition, as seen by rewriting {{math|&omega; ∧ d&omega;}} in terms of the [[Hodge star operator]] as {{math|∗⟨&omega;, ∗d&omega;⟩}}, with {{math|∗d&omega;}} being the 1-form dual to the curl vector field.{{sfnm|1a1=Choquet-Bruhat|1a2=DeWitt-Morette|1a3=Dillard-Bleick|1y=1982|1p=247}}

Hypersurface-orthogonal vector fields are particularly important in [[general relativity]], where (among other reasons) the existence of a [[Killing vector field]] which is hypersurface-orthogonal is one of the requirements of a [[static spacetime]].{{sfnm|1a1=O'Neill|1y=1983|1p=360|2a1=Stephani|2a2=Kramer|2a3=MacCallum|2a4=Hoenselaers|2y=2003|3a1=Wald|3y=1984|3loc=Section 6.1}} In this context, hypersurface-orthogonality is sometimes called ''irrotationality'', although this is in conflict with the standard usage in three dimensions.{{sfnm|1a1=O'Neill|1y=1983|1p=358}} Another name is '''rotation-freeness'''.{{sfnm|1a1=Misner|1a2=Thorne|1a3=Wheeler|1y=1973|1pp=123–124}}

An even more general notion, in the language of [[Pfaffian system]]s, is that of a [[Integrability conditions for differential systems|completely integrable 1-form]] {{math|&omega;}}, which amounts to the condition {{math|&omega; ∧ d&omega; {{=}} 0}} as given above.{{sfnm|1a1=Choquet-Bruhat|1a2=DeWitt-Morette|1a3=Dillard-Bleick|1y=1982|1loc=Section IV.C.6}} In this context, there is no metric and so there is no notion of "orthogonality".
